2	As language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises, yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
3	We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K cell-instances (140K unique passages) spanning three model families, three decoding strategies, and four depths under full-replacement chains at 1--1.5B scale.

6	Our claims hold within-strategy or when decoding configuration is known; a two-stage routing pipeline recovers $+$11.5\,pp under cross-strategy transfer.
7	Perturbation-based and membership-inference baselines lack ordinal resolution; depth estimation requires distributional statistics beyond binary detection scores.

A lightweight pipeline (19 statistical features classified by Random Forest) achieves d1--d3 balanced accuracy of 59--82\% across nine model--strategy cells, with $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70} = 3$ in 8/9 cells.
Three findings emerge: (1)~depth signal concentrates in perplexity distribution tails, corroborated by classifier convergence and independent cross-perplexity features; (2)~decoding strategy affects cross-condition transfer more than model architecture, consistent with structurally distinct degradation trajectories; (3)~signal attenuates with scale (14B: $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$ under nucleus and temperature, 0 under top-$k$), with reference-model choice as a major confound.
Our claims hold within-strategy or when decoding configuration is known; a two-stage routing pipeline recovers $+$11.5\,pp under cross-strategy transfer.
Perturbation-based and membership-inference baselines lack ordinal resolution; depth estimation requires distributional statistics beyond binary detection scores.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Definition}
5	\label{sec:method:problem}
6	
7	Let $f_\theta$ denote a language model and $\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.
8	We define a \emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\mathcal{D}_0, \mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.
9	Depth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.
10	
11	Given a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$.
12	We use \emph{depth estimation} as shorthand throughout; the underlying task is ordinal classification.
13	Depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.
14	
15	\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}
16	\label{sec:method:benchmark}
17	
18	We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.
19	
20	\paragraph{Model families.}
21	We select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).
22	Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.
23	
24	\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
25	Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
26	These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.
27	Our findings on feature importance and discriminability are limited to this grid; transfer to untested models, scales, or strategies is not established.
28	
29	\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
30	The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K cell-instances; 140K unique passages, as d0 samples are drawn from a shared Wikipedia seed corpus across all cells).
31	For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend all three models under nucleus sampling to d0--d5.
32	
33	\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
34	Starting from a Wikipedia subset ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each cycle: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ ($r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, effective batch 16, 3 epochs, dropout $0.05$; fresh adapter from the base model at each depth; full protocol in Appendix~\ref{app:lora_protocol}; cross-seed replication in Appendix~\ref{app:seed_replication}); (2)~sampling 5{,}000 passages (max 512 tokens, beginning-of-sequence (BOS) seeded; Appendix~\ref{app:length_ablation}) under the specified strategy; (3)~$\mathcal{D}_k$ feeds the next cycle.
35	Each depth is produced by a model trained on prior-depth data, not by sampling from the unmodified base model.
36	BOS seeding may amplify depth signal; prompted-generation validation (Appendix~\ref{app:prompted_gen}) confirms signal persistence albeit attenuated ($-$13.8\,pp).
37	No per-passage lineage exists across depths; cross-validation splits do not introduce leakage.
38	
39	\paragraph{Reference model.}
40	All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) use Pythia-1.4B as fixed reference model.
41	This overlaps with one generator (Pythia), conferring a 4--11\,pp self-reference advantage on that pipeline (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}); Pythia results in Table~\ref{tab:main_matrix} are marked $^\dagger$ accordingly.
42	Alternative references yield 67--79\%, all exceeding $2.5{\times}$ chance (Limitations).
43	
44	\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
45	\label{sec:method:features}
46	
47	We extract a feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ comprising 19 candidate features from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$; ablation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) shows the top 5 achieve 97.6\% of full-set performance, and variance inflation analysis reveals VIF${>}$10 for 14--16 features; effective independent dimensionality is ${\approx}$4--5.
48	The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).
49	
50	\begin{table}[t]
51	\centering
52	\small
53	\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (Pythia-1.4B).}
54	\label{tab:features}
55	\begin{tabular*}{\columnwidth}{@{\extracolsep{\fill}}llr}
56	\toprule
57	Category & Features & $n$ \\
58	\midrule
59	Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
60	statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
61	\addlinespace
62	Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
63	statistics & & \\
64	\addlinespace
65	Lexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\
66	diversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\
67	\addlinespace
68	Repetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\
69	\bottomrule
70	\end{tabular*}
71	\end{table}
72	
73	\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the per-token perplexity distribution via moments and quantiles (p10--p90); tail quantiles are especially informative as recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
74	\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features): mean, variance, and entropy of $-\log p(\text{token})$.
75	\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features): type--token ratio, hapax ratio, bigram/trigram entropy.
76	\emph{Repetition} (3 features): repeated $n$-gram fractions for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$.
77	
78	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
79	\label{sec:method:edd}
80	
81	Aggregate multi-class accuracy obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depth boundaries.
82	We propose the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) as an operational measure of how far into a recursive chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.
83	
84	\paragraph{Pairwise discriminability.}
85	Let $\mathcal{D} = \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$ denote the depth set and $T \in (0.5, 1.0]$ a discrimination threshold.
86	For each adjacent pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we define the pairwise discriminability $\mathrm{AUC}(d, d{+}1)$ as the area under the ROC curve of a dedicated binary Random Forest classifier (500 trees, $\lfloor\sqrt{19}\rfloor$ candidate features per split) trained on class-balanced data from $\mathbf{f}(x)$ (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) to distinguish depth-$d$ from depth-$(d{+}1)$ samples, evaluated via 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
87	Each pair uses an independent classifier to avoid decision boundary dilution from multi-class settings.
88	
89	\begin{definition}[Effective Discriminable Depth]
90	\label{def:edd}
91	The \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} at threshold $T$ is:
92	\begin{multline}
93	\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \bigl\{ d^*{+}1 \,:\, \\
94	\forall\, d' \leq d^*,\; \mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \geq T \bigr\}
95	\label{eq:edd}
96	\end{multline}
97	where $d^* \in \{0, \dots, K{-}1\}$. If\, $\mathrm{AUC}(0,1) < T$, then $\mathrm{EDD}_T = 0$.
98	\end{definition}
99	
100	$\mathrm{EDD}_T$ reports the longest \emph{contiguous} discriminable prefix: the deepest $d$ such that every pair from $(0,1)$ through $(d{-}1, d)$ exceeds $T$.
101	All AUC profiles in the primary benchmark decay monotonically; non-monotonic profiles occur only in cross-scale extensions (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_full}).
102	We adopt $T{=}0.70$ following the ``acceptable discrimination'' threshold in ROC analysis \cite{hosmer2000} (8/9 cells achieve $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70} \geq 3$); sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) shows $\mathrm{EDD}$ shifts by at most one level across $T \in \{0.65, 0.70, 0.80\}$ in all nine cells.
103	
104	\paragraph{Classifiers.}
105	Our primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold CV; EDD binary classifiers use 500 trees; seed robustness in Appendix~\ref{app:rf_seed}).\footnote{Statistical tests are not corrected for multiple comparisons; $p$-values should be interpreted as exploratory.}
106	The RF produces ordinally consistent predictions: 98.2\% of errors fall on adjacent depths ($|\Delta| \leq 1$), quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)\,=\,0.89.
107	Comparisons against other classifiers and detection baselines appear in \S\ref{sec:generalization}.

1	\subsection{Theoretical Motivation}
2	\label{sec:method:theory}
3	
4	Recursive generation contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first \cite{shumailov2024_nature}: tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in depth $k$.
5	This tail erosion predicts the perplexity tail feature family as a depth marker, confirmed jointly with surprisal variance across all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}).
6	Surprisal variance captures complementary distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.
7	
8	\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
9	Tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\gamma^k$ for a contraction factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$ \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below classifier resolution.
10	Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay approaching a fixed point \cite{bertrand2024_stability}.
11	5-class extensions to d4 (71--81\%, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm depth~4 discriminability; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics, placing a physical ceiling on EDD.
12	
13	\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
14	Larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step ($\gamma$ closer to 1), predicting weaker per-step signal.
15	Qwen2.5-14B supports this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.98$ at 1--1.5B; \S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}); 7--8B results are mixed, and additional confounds likely interact with the scale effect (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_full}).
16	
17	\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
18	The contraction rate $\gamma$ varies with decoding strategy.
19	Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
20	GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3).
21	Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Four importance measures converge on the same ranking (Kendall's $W{=}0.90$); Binoculars cross-perplexity features independently reach 78.1\% (merged: 82.6\%; Appendix~\ref{app:feature_ablation_bino}); four classifiers converge within 0.8\,pp (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}); CORAL adds $+$0.3\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:learned_estimator}).
The accuracy ceiling thus resides in the feature space, not the classifier.
End-to-end classifiers lag by 14--33\,pp (d2 F1\,${\leq}$\,0.26; Appendix~\ref{app:e2e}, \ref{app:dcol_iterations}), likely because depth signal resides in passage-level distributional tail statistics rather than local coherence patterns.
The strategy effect (9.3\,pp) exceeds the model effect (7.2\,pp), so deployment requires conditioning on decoding configuration (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}); the fixed reference model degrades by 4--11\,pp under cross-architecture alternatives (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}), and a 7B self-reference probe reveals a scale-dependent ceiling ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}0$; Appendix~\ref{app:qwen7b_selfref}).
Accumulation experiments and cross-boundary chains (84.8\%; Appendix~\ref{app:accumulation_auc},~\ref{app:cross_boundary}) indicate that depth fingerprints are process-level rather than model-specific.

In summary, recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints that a lightweight pipeline resolves into ordinal depth classes ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}3$ in 8/9 cells), enabling more targeted data filtering than binary detection for provenance auditing and collapse monitoring.
Open questions include reference-model alignment beyond 1.5B (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}), paraphrase robustness, and finer-grained mixing (\S\ref{sec:gen:accumulation}).

39	\label{app:topk_trajectories}

41	Feature trajectories for nucleus and temperature sampling appear in Figure~\ref{fig:feature_trajectory} (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).
42	Top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) trajectories follow the same monotonically decreasing trend for all features but with compressed inter-depth spacing, consistent with the signal attenuation effect discussed in \S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}.
43	Concretely, the d0$\to$d1 drop in \texttt{p90\_ppl} under top-$k$ is 78\% (vs.\ 87\% for nucleus), and the d2$\to$d3 reduction is 31\% (vs.\ 39\% for nucleus).
44	Despite the magnitude reduction, feature rank ordering across depths is preserved, which explains why ordinal classifiers maintain directionality even under top-$k$ conditions.

46	\subsection{Permutation Importance}
47	\label{app:permutation}
48	
49	To verify that the Gini-based importance rankings in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features} are not an artifact of the impurity measure, we compute permutation importance (5-fold CV, 10 repeats) for all 9 atlas cells.
50	The top-2 features are stable across measures: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in 9/9 cells under both Gini and permutation importance, and \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 (vs.\ 7/9 for Gini, with the additional cell being OLMo top-$k$; the single SHAP exception is GPT-2~XL top-$k$, where \texttt{p75\_ppl} displaces \texttt{var\_surprisal} to rank 3).
51	Kendall's $W{=}0.90$ across all three methods (Gini, permutation, SHAP) indicates strong concordance ($p{<}0.005$).
52	Pairwise Spearman correlations are: SHAP--Gini $\rho{=}0.93$, SHAP--permutation $\rho{=}0.84$, Gini--permutation $\rho{=}0.76$.

56	\label{app:conditional_pi}

60	
61	\paragraph{Setup.}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models (LLMs) are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical; it is already occurring in the wild. Yet whether the recursive generation depth of a text can be estimated from its statistical properties remains unstudied, a question that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
We focus on the 1--1.5B parameter regime under \emph{controlled full-replacement chains}, where each generation fully replaces the prior training set, isolating the depth variable. Real-world contamination involves partial mixing at unknown proportions; full replacement provides an upper bound on depth signal strength (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors \cite{binoculars2024,fast_detectgpt2024,diveye2026} collapse all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category, a limitation we confirm empirically: their pairwise d1-vs-d2 AUC collapses to chance level (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}); watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone (Figure~\ref{fig:problem}).

We find that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{consistent in direction but scale-dependent in magnitude} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, the perplexity tail feature family (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{p75\_ppl}, \texttt{kurtosis\_ppl}) and surprisal variance emerge as dominant depth indicators, with group-level dominance robust across all 9 model--strategy configurations and three importance measures.
Our contribution centers on task formalization and systematic empirical characterization; the convergence of four classifiers within 0.8\,pp (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}) confirms that signal resides in feature design, not classifier architecture.
We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and find that a lightweight pipeline suffices: compute 19 reference-model statistical features (effective dimensionality ${\approx}$4--5 due to multicollinearity; \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) and classify with a Random Forest into $K{+}1$ depth classes.
To characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families $\times$ decoding strategies spanning 4 depths (180K cell-instances).
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories; we introduce \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Perturbation-based and membership-inference baselines lack ordinal resolution; depth estimation requires distributional statistics beyond binary detection scores.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models (LLMs) are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical; it is already occurring in the wild. Yet whether the recursive generation depth of a text can be estimated from its statistical properties remains unstudied, a question that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
We focus on the 1--1.5B parameter regime under \emph{controlled full-replacement chains}, where each generation fully replaces the prior training set, isolating the depth variable. Real-world contamination involves partial mixing at unknown proportions; full replacement provides an upper bound on depth signal strength (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors \cite{binoculars2024,fast_detectgpt2024,diveye2026} collapse all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category, a limitation we confirm empirically: their pairwise d1-vs-d2 AUC collapses to chance level (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}); watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone (Figure~\ref{fig:problem}).

We find that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{consistent in direction but scale-dependent in magnitude} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, the perplexity tail feature family (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{p75\_ppl}, \texttt{kurtosis\_ppl}) and surprisal variance emerge as dominant depth indicators, with group-level dominance robust across all 9 model--strategy configurations and three importance measures.
Our contribution centers on task formalization and systematic empirical characterization; the convergence of four classifiers within 0.8\,pp (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}) confirms that signal resides in feature design, not classifier architecture.
We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and find that a lightweight pipeline suffices: compute 19 reference-model statistical features (effective dimensionality ${\approx}$4--5 due to multicollinearity; \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) and classify with a Random Forest (RF) into $K{+}1$ depth classes.
To characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families $\times$ decoding strategies spanning 4 depths (180K cell-instances).
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories; we introduce \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_problem_illustration.pdf}
\caption{Recursive generation depth estimation. A seed corpus $\mathcal{D}_0$ feeds a LoRA finetuning--sampling loop producing successively deeper corpora. Given a passage~$x$, the task is to estimate its ordinal depth~$d$.}
\label{fig:problem}
\end{figure*}
Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formalization and metric.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, and construct a 180K cell-instance benchmark ($3$ model families $\times$ $3$ decoding strategies $\times$ $4$ depths; 140K unique passages).

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} The perplexity tail feature family and surprisal variance jointly dominate depth discrimination across all 9 cells; $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}3$ in 8/9 cells (4 under nucleus depth extension), validated by 5-class extension (71--81\%); feature group ablation confirms perplexity tail dominance (76.6\% alone vs.\ 78.4\% full set).

    \item \textbf{Partial-mixing validation.} Under 25--50\% synthetic mixing, $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}3$ is preserved in 5/6 cells with $-$8--15\,pp accuracy attenuation.

    \item \textbf{Generalization boundaries.} Within the tested 1--1.5B regime, cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-domain (arXiv) 74.1\%; at 14B, cross-reference $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$; cross-strategy (d1--d3: 45.9\%) is a boundary condition, partially recovered by two-stage routing ($+$11.5\,pp).
\end{itemize}

\begin{abstract}
As language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises, yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K cell-instances (140K unique passages) spanning three model families, three decoding strategies, and four depths under full-replacement chains at 1--1.5B scale.
A lightweight pipeline (19 statistical features classified by Random Forest) achieves d1--d3 balanced accuracy of 59--82\% across nine model--strategy cells, with Effective Discriminable Depth $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70} = 3$ in 8/9 cells.
Three findings emerge: (1)~depth signal concentrates in perplexity distribution tails, corroborated by classifier convergence and independent cross-perplexity features; (2)~decoding strategy affects cross-condition transfer more than model architecture, consistent with structurally distinct degradation trajectories; (3)~signal attenuates with scale (14B: $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$ under nucleus and temperature, 0 under top-$k$), with reference-model choice as a major confound.
Our claims hold within-strategy or when decoding configuration is known; a two-stage routing pipeline recovers $+$11.5\,pp under cross-strategy transfer.
Perturbation-based and membership-inference baselines lack ordinal resolution; depth estimation requires distributional statistics beyond binary detection scores.
\end{abstract}

# Paper Banana — 高品质学术概念图生成

PaperBanana 由 Gemini Pro 自动写 matplotlib 代码，VLM Critic 评估渲染结果并迭代优化，输出顶会级别 300 DPI 概念图。

**质量底线：每张图必须达到顶会论文的美观度——高级感、专业感、精致感。绝不接受 matplotlib 默认样式的廉价感。**

## 适用范围

| 场景 | 用什么 |
|------|--------|
| **概念图**（架构图、流程图、framework 示意） | **PaperBanana** ← 本 skill |
| **统计图**（scatter、bar、line、heatmap、forest） | **draw-paper-figure.skill.md**。**不要用 PaperBanana 画统计图** |
| 离线 / 无 GOOGLE_API_KEY | **draw-paper-figure.skill.md** |

## 执行环境

**PaperBanana 在本机（EC2）运行，不要 SSH 到远程服务器。**

EC2（ap-northeast-1 东京）可直接访问 Gemini API，无需代理。

## 前置条件

### Step 1：获取 GOOGLE_API_KEY

```python
request_secret(key_id="google_api_key", project="<project_name>", purpose="PaperBanana 概念图生成")
# 等待 Director 审批后
poll_secret_request(request_id="<返回的 request_id>", project="<project_name>")
```

如果密钥尚未存储，告知 Director 需要 GOOGLE_API_KEY。

### Step 2：安装验证（每次使用前必须检查）

```bash
# 检查是否已安装
paperbanana --version 2>/dev/null || {
  echo "PaperBanana 未安装，正在安装..."
  pip install paperbanana -q
  paperbanana --version
}
```

如果 `paperbanana --version` 失败（命令不存在），必须先 `pip install paperbanana -q` 安装。版本需 ≥ 0.1.2。

**设计前必读** `skills/global/paper-visualization.skill.md` 的概念图 L1（防丑 7 条）+ L2（叙事 6 条）+ L3 Pattern + Checklist。统计图部分不适用于 PaperBanana。

## 命令：generate

概念图用 `generate` 子命令。**必须显式指定 `--vlm-model gemini-2.5-pro`**（默认模型 `gemini-2.0-flash` 已废弃，不指定会崩溃）。**`--iterations 5`**。

## 完整流程

### Step 1：写意图描述文件

将详细设计描述写入文件（太长不适合命令行参数）：

```bash
cat > /tmp/fig_intent.txt << 'INTENT'
Three-panel academic figure for a top-venue paper (full width, aspect ratio ~3.2:1, figsize 14x4.5 inches):

Panel (a) 'The Phenomenon' (left, ~38% width):
Grouped bar chart. TF bars: dark navy (#2C3E50). AR bars: academic red (#C0392B).
Exact data: Base TF=0.501 AR=0.019, ThreadGate TF=0.504 AR=0.064, ...
Y-axis 'Mid-turn GAR' range 0–0.55. Only left+bottom spines. Serif font 10pt.
Add bracket annotation '8-17x gap' between bar groups.

Panel (b) 'Diagnostic Chain' (center, ~24% width):
Vertical flowchart, 4 rounded boxes connected by thin gray arrows:
  Step 1: light gray (#F5F6F7) box, thin border (#DEE2E6), 'Gate Analysis' + subtitle. Green ✓
  Step 2: same style, 'PCGrad Exclusion'. Red ✗
  Step 3: same style, 'Representation Check'. Red ✗
  Step 4: light green (#D4EDDA) background, 'Conclusion: Exposure bias'. Green ✓
No axes, no spines. Clean infographic style.

Panel (c) 'Constructive Evidence' (right, ~38% width):
Line plot. Data points: (0, 0.064), (3, 0.556), (5, 0.727).
Navy line (#2C3E50), open circles (white fill, navy edge, width 2).
Light blue fill (#EBF5FB, alpha 0.4) under curve.
Annotate '11x recovery' in muted gray, 9pt italic.

OVERALL STYLE:
- 300 DPI, white background, publication quality
- Serif font (Times New Roman or similar) throughout
- Panel labels '(a)', '(b)', '(c)' in 11pt bold at top-left
- Generous white space (wspace=0.35)
- Muted academic palette: navy #2C3E50, red #C0392B, green #27AE60, gray #7F8C8D
- NO matplotlib default styling: no gray background, no thick gridlines, no tab10 colors
- Drop shadows on boxes: subtle, 2px offset, 10% opacity
- Rounded corners 8px on all rectangles
- Arrow heads: small, elegant, not bulky
INTENT
```

### Step 2：运行 generate

```bash
GOOGLE_API_KEY="[REDACTED]" paperbanana generate \
  --input /tmp/fig_intent.txt \
  --caption "Three-panel diagnostic framework: (a) TF vs AR performance gap, (b) systematic diagnosis chain, (c) beta-steering recovery evidence" \
  --vlm-model gemini-2.5-pro \
  --output figures/paper/fig1_overview.png \
  --iterations 5
```

### Step 3：视觉检查（不可跳过）

**Read 生成的 PNG 文件**，视觉评估以下维度：

1. **高级感**：是否有顶会论文的精致感？还是看起来像课程作业？
2. **颜色**：是否有语义（不是随机分配）？是否和谐、不刺眼？
3. **文字**：缩到 column width 后是否 ≥ 7pt 可读？
4. **布局**：留白是否合理？元素是否对齐？
5. **细节**：圆角、阴影、箭头是否精致？边框是否统一？

**不满意 → 必须修改意图描述文件，重新生成。**

### Step 4：转 PDF

```bash
python3 -c "
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, matplotlib.image as mpimg
img = mpimg.imread('figures/paper/fig1_overview.png')
h, w = img.shape[:2]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(w/300, h/300), dpi=300)
ax = fig.add_axes([0,0,1,1]); ax.imshow(img); ax.axis('off')
plt.savefig('figures/paper/fig1_overview.pdf', bbox_inches='tight', pad_inches=0)
plt.close()
"
```

## 意图描述质量红线

Intent 质量直接决定图的质量。必须包含以下 7 项（缺一不可）：

1. **空间布局**：每个 panel 的宽度占比（如 38%/24%/38%）
2. **组件形状 + 尺寸**：圆角半径 8px、figsize (14, 4.5)
3. **颜色 hex 码**：不说"蓝色"，说 "#2C3E50"，绑定语义
4. **所有文字内容**：box label、副标题、箭头 annotation
5. **尺寸规格**：DPI 300、字号 10-12pt body / 8-9pt labels
6. **细节规格**：阴影偏移 2px / 10% opacity、箭头粗细、边框宽度
7. **反面约束**："NO matplotlib default styling, NO gray background, NO tab10 colors"

### 美学风格关键词（必须在 intent 中出现）

```
STYLE REQUIREMENTS:
- Publication quality for a TOP venue (NeurIPS/ICML/EMNLP)
- Elegant, premium, sophisticated — NOT cheap or homework-like
- Subtle drop shadows (2px, 10% opacity) on boxes
- Rounded corners (8px) on all rectangles
- Thin, elegant arrow heads — not bulky matplotlib defaults
- Serif font (Times) for labels, sans-serif (Helvetica) for annotations
- Muted, harmonious color palette — NO saturated primary colors
- Generous white space between elements
- Consistent visual weight across all panels
```

### 反面教材（这样的 intent 一定画不好）

- "Draw a pipeline diagram with three stages"
- "Architecture diagram for our system"

太模糊。LLM 会用 matplotlib 默认样式填充所有你没指定的细节，结果就是廉价感。

## 迭代策略（至少 3 轮外部迭代，Hero Figure 至少 5 轮）

PaperBanana 内部有 VLM Critic 迭代（`--iterations 5`），但这还不够。你必须做**外部迭代**：

### 第 1 轮：基础生成
运行 PaperBanana → Read PNG → 识别大方向问题（布局、配色、结构）

### 第 2 轮：结构修复
修改意图描述（布局占比、颜色 hex、组件关系）→ 重新运行 → Read PNG

### 第 3 轮：细节打磨
修改意图描述（字号、阴影、对齐、箭头粗细）→ 重新运行 → Read PNG

### 第 4 轮（Hero Figure）：风格统一
线宽 / 字号 / 间距全图统一？与论文其他图配色一致？→ 重新运行 → Read PNG

### 第 5 轮（Hero Figure）：最终 polish
像素级检查 → 缩到 column width 后文字 ≥ 7pt？→ 终极判断：放在 NeurIPS best paper 里违和吗？

### 判断标准

**可以交付**：看起来像 NeurIPS 2025 best paper 里的图。
**不可交付**：看起来像 matplotlib gallery 的示例图。

## 失败回退

如果 PaperBanana 多次崩溃（API 错误、模型不兼容）：

1. 确认 `--vlm-model gemini-2.5-pro` 是否指定
2. 确认 GOOGLE_API_KEY 是否有效：`curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models?key=$GOOGLE_API_KEY"` 应返回 200
3. 如果仍然失败，回退 matplotlib 手写：
   - Read `skills/global/paper-visualization.skill.md` 获取 L1-L4 设计标准
   - 写 Python 脚本手动画概念图（FancyBboxPatch、FancyArrowPatch 等）
   - **同样必须 Read PNG 做视觉检查，至少迭代 3 轮**
   - **同样必须达到顶会级别的美观度**
   - 保存 .py 脚本到 figures/paper/ 目录便于后续修改

\label{sec:method:edd}

Aggregate multi-class accuracy obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depth boundaries.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
Recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails \cite{shumailov2024_nature}, an effect formalized as exponential tail decay via scaling laws \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails,seddik2024synthetic} and extended to autophagous loops in the MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} and Markovian generation chains \cite{geng2026_markovian}.
Subsequent work refines the conditions under which collapse occurs: \citet{bertrand2024_stability} identify convergence to a fixed point under mixed real-synthetic retraining (providing theoretical grounding for our EDD ceiling, \S\ref{sec:method:theory}), \citet{shi2025_closer_look} reframe collapse as a generalization-to-memorization transition, and \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} extend guarantees to broader model classes.
Mitigation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate,drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse,yi2026_escaping_collapse,falahati2026_curated}, convergence analysis \cite{marchi2024_heat_death,wang2026_contamination,dohmatob2024_demystified,suresh2025_rate_collapse}, non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement,kazdan2025_collapse_or_thrive}, and diversity decline \cite{guo2024curious,padmakumar2024diversity,sigma2026_spectral} are active areas.
\citet{schaeffer2025} argue that ``model collapse'' conflates multiple phenomena and call for operationally precise metrics; we respond by operationalizing tail-erosion predictions into a deployable ordinal classifier that reveals strategy-dependent trajectories and non-monotonic 7B behavior that the theory does not predict.
All assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
The detection literature \cite{wu2025_detection_survey} spans statistical \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt,fast_detectgpt2024,binoculars2024,diveye2026,guo2024_biscope,gehrmann2019_gltr,verma2024_ghostbuster,yang2024_dnagpt}, geometric \cite{tulchinskii2023_intrinsic_dim}, and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} methods, with known limits \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase,pudasaini2026_detection_fails,pu2026_generator_barrier}.
\citet{wang2023_seqxgpt} address sentence-level attribution by using log-probability features from white-box LLMs.
Shared tasks \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval,li2024_mage,bevendorff2026_pan,dugan2024_raid} benchmark detection across domains and attack vectors.
\citet{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms} distinguish attribution from verification; depth estimation introduces a third axis: recursive iteration.
All perform binary classification; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing detection.

\paragraph{Membership Inference and Data Provenance.}
\citet{carlini2021_extracting} demonstrate that training data can be extracted from LLMs, motivating provenance-aware pipelines.
Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} detects pretraining membership via low-probability token statistics, related to our perplexity features but limited to binary classification; Datamodels \cite{ilyas2022datamodels} trace predictions to influential training examples; cryptographically undetectable watermarks \cite{christ2024_undetectable} require generator cooperation.
TROVE \cite{zhu2025_trove} introduces fine-grained sentence-level provenance tracing with relationship classification, but targets source attribution rather than recursive depth.
Depth estimation occupies a distinct niche: ordinal, retroactive, and cooperation-free.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains; \citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text; \citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} characterize \emph{how} text degrades under iterative generation without classifying which iteration a passage comes from.
Our task performs the inverse: ordinal depth estimation from text alone.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses; \citet{kasa2024_ordinality} benchmark ordinal techniques for NLP; \citet{janitza2016_ordinal_rf} show RF implicitly respects ordinal structure when inter-class distances are monotonic.
We adopt CORAL and CLOC as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus,finlayson2024_closing,garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded,wiher2022_decoding,basu2021_mirostat}.
Our atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) shows these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation.

We probe whether end-to-end PLM representations capture the same depth signals as our statistical features via linear probing of [CLS] representations from DeBERTa-v3-base and RoBERTa-base.

-PLM representations excel at surface lexical features (TTR: $R^2{=}0.85$, repeated bigrams) but fail to capture perplexity distribution statistics; \texttt{var\_surprisal} and \texttt{p90\_ppl} yield negative $R^2$ under linear probing; these features are not linearly accessible in the pretrained representation space.

+PLM representations excel at surface lexical features (type--token ratio (TTR): $R^2{=}0.85$, repeated bigrams) but fail to capture perplexity distribution statistics; \texttt{var\_surprisal} and \texttt{p90\_ppl} yield negative $R^2$ under linear probing; these features are not linearly accessible in the pretrained representation space.

This confirms that the 20pp accuracy gap between feature-based and end-to-end methods (\S\ref{app:e2e}) stems from complementary, not redundant, representations: PLMs capture lexical patterns while the targeted statistical features capture distributional tail properties that constitute the dominant depth markers.
